turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. I’m here because... man, I just don't know what to do anymore. It’s like, I feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin whenever I’m supposed to just sit still. And it’s really becoming a huge problem, especially with my classes and my clinicals. 

I'm in school to be a radiologic tech, right? And in the radiology suite, there's a lot of waiting around, sitting behind the glass while the scans are running, or just sitting in these long lectures for my college classes. And I just... I can't do it. I mean, I’ve been trying so hard to just tough it out. For months now, I've been telling myself to just sit in the chair, just be normal, don't move. But the tension just builds and builds in my legs and my arms until I feel like I'm going to explode if I don't get up. 

So I always end up pacing around the control room, or shifting constantly in my seat until the professor or the head tech looks at me, or I'm always finding some random excuse to get up and move. Like, I'll pretend I need to go organize the lead aprons, or I'll go to the bathroom three times in an hour, or I'll just stand in the back of the classroom and pretend my back hurts. It's exhausting, honestly, because I'm trying to be professional and learn the equipment, but my body just will not let me just sit there. I just can't turn it off, no matter how hard I try to just stay put.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient reports shifting constantly in their seat when expected to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes frequently leaving their seat in class or the radiology suite by finding random excuses to get up and move.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes an intense internal feeling of restlessness, stating they feel like they are 'crawling out of my skin' and that tension builds until they feel they will explode if they don't move.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?
turns.patient_response:
Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess I stress about normal stuff sometimes, like passing my radiographic physics class, because that class is honestly a complete nightmare. You have to memorize all these formulas for kilovoltage peak and scatter radiation, and the professor is this super strict guy who expects you to just know everything perfectly and sit there for two hours straight while he drones on. But it's not like I'm sitting around constantly fretting about a million different things, you know? 

Like, I'm not lying awake at night agonizing over my future or my finances or what somebody said to me three weeks ago or anything like that. It's not a mental spinning. It's really just this intense physical need to move. Like, my brain isn't filled with anxious thoughts, it's just constantly yelling at my muscles to do something. 

My mom is a huge worrier, actually—she'll call me twice a day just to ask if I checked my tire pressure or if I'm eating enough protein or if I locked my apartment door, and I always tell her I'm fine, I don't even think about that stuff. I just don't really have that worry gene, I guess. If I'm up and walking around, I feel totally fine mentally. It's just the physical act of being trapped in a chair that makes me feel like I'm going insane, not actual worry about life stuff. So, yeah, no, I wouldn't say I worry a lot about different things.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense physical need to move and feeling like they are going insane when trapped in a chair.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly denies lying awake at night agonizing over things.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies worrying a lot about many different things, stating they do not fret about a million different things.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have trouble staying focused on lectures or tasks because your mind drifts off?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly, I don't really have that problem. Like, my mind isn't drifting off to, you know, what I'm gonna have for dinner or some movie I saw last weekend or whatever. It's actually the opposite, kind of? I'm trying so hard to focus on the lecture, like when we're learning about the different contrast agents, barium versus iodine, which is super important because you can literally kill someone if you use the wrong one if they have a perforation, right? So I know I need to pay attention. And I *am* paying attention. I hear everything the professor is saying. 

But it's just... the whole time I'm listening, my body is just screaming at me to move. So I'm sitting there, and I'm taking notes, and my handwriting gets all messy because I'm tapping my pen so hard, or I'm bouncing my leg up and down under the desk so fast that the person next to me usually gives me this annoyed look. And I'm fully aware of the lecture, I'm tracking with the material, I'm just doing it while feeling like I'm trapped in a cage. 

It's not that I zone out. I don't daydream. I don't sit there staring blankly at the wall. I'm very present. It's just that being present requires this massive amount of physical restraint that I just don't have. So, yeah, the focusing part isn't the issue, it's just the sitting still part that completely ruins the experience for me. If I could just stand at the back of the room and pace back and forth while he talks about the inverse square law, I'd probably get an A in the class, you know? But they don't really let you do that. So I just suffer in the chair. But no, my mind doesn't drift.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling like they are trapped in a cage and that their body is screaming at them to move when forced to sit still.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself interrupting people or blurting things out before they finish?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man. Yeah. Yes, absolutely. It's honestly one of the most embarrassing things that happens to me at clinicals. Like, I do it all the time, and I hate that I do it, but I just can't seem to stop myself. 

Like, okay, for example, just last week, I was in the fluoroscopy room with my clinical instructor, Mr. Davis. He's this older guy, super experienced, been a tech for like thirty years, and he's great, but he talks kind of slow. So we were getting ready for a barium enema, which is a really involved procedure, you know, you have to have the room set up perfectly, the contrast mixed right, the fluoroscopy tower in the right position, all the lead aprons ready for the radiologist. And Mr. Davis was going over the protocol with me before the patient came in. 

He was starting to explain how he wanted me to position the patient for the left lateral decubitus view, and he's like, "Now, when we roll the patient onto their left side, I want you to make sure you grab the..." and before he even finished the sentence, my brain just fired off, and I blurted out, "The high-density barium! I got it, I'll grab the bag!" And I just completely cut him off. 

And he just stopped and looked at me, and he was like, "No, I was going to say, grab the extra radiolucent sponges to build them up so we don't clip the dependent side of the colon on the image." And I just felt like such an idiot. Because, first of all, the contrast was already hanging on the IV pole, so my answer didn't even make sense in context, but my brain was just racing ahead, trying to anticipate what he was going to say, and the words just fell out of my mouth before I could even process them. 

And it happens when they ask me questions, too. Like, a supervisor will be quizzing me, like, "What's the central ray angle for an AP axial Towne method of the skull?" and they'll be in the middle of saying "Towne method," and I'm already yelling out "Thirty degrees caudad to the OML!" And then they'll finish the question and be like, "...if the IOML is perpendicular to the image receptor." Which changes the answer to thirty-seven degrees, right? But I already jumped in with the wrong answer because I couldn't just wait two more seconds for them to finish the sentence. 

It's like I have this physical pressure in my chest when someone is talking, especially if they're explaining something I think I already know or if I'm eager to prove I know it, and the pressure just forces the words out. I interrupt my friends, I interrupt my mom, I interrupt the techs... and then I realize I missed the part that actually mattered, the crucial detail at the end of their sentence, and I end up looking careless or like I'm not listening. But I am listening! I'm just listening too fast, if that makes sense? So, yeah, blurting things out is a huge, huge problem for me. It's definitely something I do way too often.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they frequently blurt out answers before questions or sentences are finished, providing specific examples from their clinicals.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient confirms they frequently interrupt others, stating 'I interrupt my friends, I interrupt my mom, I interrupt the techs'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have this same need to move around when you're at home, like during meals or while relaxing?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, absolutely. It's not just a school thing or a clinical thing. It's everywhere. Even when I'm at home and I'm supposed to be, you know, "relaxing." Like, sitting at the dinner table is practically a workout. My mom is always sighing because I'm shaking the whole table with my leg bouncing, so honestly, half the time I just eat standing up at the kitchen counter so I don't have to deal with sitting. 

But it's weird because it even happens when I'm doing stuff I actually *want* to do to relax. Like, I'm really into photography, and I do a lot of photo editing, and I also like sketching. You'd think those are supposed to be these quiet, chill activities, right? Like, you just sit at your desk, put on some music, and draw or edit. But I literally cannot keep it quiet for long. It's impossible for me. 

I'll sit down to edit a batch of photos on my laptop, and within maybe three or four minutes, I start tapping my mouse or my pen on the desk. Or I'll start humming—usually just the same five seconds of a song on a loop without even realizing it. And if there's anyone else around, like if my mom is in the room or if I'm doing this in the computer lab at school, I just start talking to whoever's nearby. I'll just start narrating what I'm doing, or I'll ask them some totally random question that popped into my head, just because I can't stand the silence. 

And the getting up... man, I get up *so* much. I'll edit one photo, stand up, pace around the room, go open the fridge, realize I'm not even hungry, close it, walk back, sketch two lines on my paper, and then stand up again to look out the window. It drives everyone around me completely crazy. People at home, or the other students in the lab, they're constantly having to tell me to just settle down. They'll be like, "Dude, can you please stop tapping?" or "Can you just sit in your chair for ten consecutive minutes?" And I always feel bad because I don't even realize I'm being that loud or restless until they point it out. I just... I really can't do quiet. Even when I'm having fun, my body just refuses to be still and quiet at the same time.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes bouncing their leg enough to shake the dinner table and constantly tapping their mouse or pen.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient frequently leaves their seat, eating standing up to avoid sitting and constantly getting up to pace while trying to do desk activities.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient explicitly states they cannot engage in relaxing leisure activities like sketching or photo editing quietly, as they inevitably start humming, talking, or moving.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often have trouble finishing tasks once you start them?
turns.patient_response:
No, actually, I don't think I really have that issue. Like, if I start something, I definitely finish it. It's not like I just leave a trail of half-done projects everywhere, you know? I mean, the process of getting it done might look like a complete tornado just ripped through the room, but the actual task gets finished. 

Like, for example, in our positioning lab last Tuesday, we had to do a complete hand series on the phantoms—PA, PA oblique, and lateral. And you have to get everything perfect, right? The SID has to be exactly forty inches, you have to collimate down to just the hand and wrist so you aren't radiating the whole table, you have to place the right lead marker... and I do all of it. I don't just do the PA view and then wander off and forget about the rest of the exam. I finish the whole series. Every single time. 

I mean, sure, I might be literally sprinting back and forth between the x-ray tube and the control panel, and I'm probably tapping my lead marker against the table the whole time I'm trying to line up the central ray with the third MCP joint, but I get the job done. I don't quit halfway. 

And it's the exact same thing with my homework. Like, we have these massive workbook assignments for our radiation physics class, which is just brutally boring, honestly. It's all these formulas for mAs and kVp and calculating the fifteen percent rule and inverse square law stuff. And I don't just do half a page and say forget it and leave it. I actually power through the whole entire chapter. Now, granted, I might have to stand up and pace around my kitchen island like twenty times while I'm doing it, and my leg is probably bouncing so hard the whole time that my knee hurts by the end of the night, but the workbook gets completely filled out. 

So, yeah, getting to the finish line isn't really my problem at all. I always get to the end of whatever I'm supposed to be doing. It's just... the actual journey of getting to that finish line is incredibly restless and loud and chaotic, I guess. But no, I definitely finish what I start.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly denies leaving tasks half-done, stating they always finish their projects and homework.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes tapping their lead marker against the table and bouncing their leg constantly.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions having to stand up and pace around the kitchen island multiple times while doing homework.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling 'incredibly restless' and mentions sprinting back and forth and pacing to get things done.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have this same difficulty staying still when you’re doing something active, like exercising or walking around?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's funny you ask that, because my entire life is basically just one giant active thing. Like, I don't really give myself the chance to even try to be still, because I just... I never stop moving. 

Most days, I literally go straight from my morning classes—like, say I have radiographic pathology or anatomy at 8 AM—and the second the professor dismisses us, I'm practically sprinting to my car to get to my clinical rotation at the hospital. And at clinicals, I'm on my feet the entire shift, right? I'm pushing the portable x-ray machine all the way across the hospital to the ICU, I'm helping slide patients onto the imaging table, I'm running back and forth to the control booth. I am constantly in motion. 

But then, the minute my shift is over, I don't go home and put my feet up. I go straight to the gym. And even at the gym, I'm the guy who can't just sit on the bench and look at his phone between sets. I'm pacing around the weight room, I'm doing calf raises, I'm walking across the gym to the water fountain and back, just constantly moving. And then after the gym, it's straight to running errands. I'll go to the grocery store, I'll go get gas, I'll go wash my car, I'll go buy new scrub tops. I just bounce from class to clinicals to the gym to errands without really stopping at all. 

And it's like... if there is ever a gap in my schedule? Like, say a patient no-shows at clinicals, or a professor lets us out of lecture twenty minutes early? I immediately have to fill it with something. I can't just go sit in the breakroom or hang out in the library and chill. I'll be like, "Okay, I have twenty free minutes, I'm going to go walk up and down the stairwell," or "I'm going to go reorganize the lead aprons on the rack," or I'll just start doing laps around the hospital wing. Because sitting around just feels... it's almost impossible for me. It genuinely feels terrible. It's like my body is an engine that's just revving at the redline all day, so I have to keep it in drive, you know? If I put it in park, the whole thing just shakes and feels wrong. So yeah, I just link all these active things together all day long so I never actually have to deal with trying to be still.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense internal feeling of restlessness, stating that sitting around feels 'almost impossible' and 'genuinely feels terrible.'
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly describes being constantly in motion, going from activity to activity without stopping, and compares their body to 'an engine that's just revving at the redline all day,' which perfectly matches acting as if driven by a motor.

turns.doctor_question: Were you like this as a child, before age 12?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, yeah. 100 percent. Like, this is definitely not just some new thing that started because I'm stressed about clinicals or my radiology training or whatever. It's been my whole life. My parents actually still bring it up all the time—well, I mean, it's probably more like a traumatic memory for them at this point, but they still talk about my parent-teacher conferences back in elementary school. Like, we're talking way, way before middle school. First grade, second grade, third grade, it was literally the exact same story every single year. 

They'd go in for the conference, sit in those tiny little plastic chairs in my classroom, and the teachers would just unload on them about how I was literally always out of my seat. Like, the teacher would just turn around to write the date on the whiteboard, and I'd already be up wandering over to the pencil sharpener or going to look out the window or messing with the class hamster. 

And the calling out... oh my gosh, I was so bad about that. I just could not raise my hand and wait to be called on. It physically hurt to hold it in. If I knew the answer, or honestly even if I just had a totally random thought about whatever we were reading, I'd just shout it out in the middle of the room. The teachers were constantly writing notes home about it. 

They also told my parents I was always rushing ahead before the directions were even finished. Like, the teacher would be passing out a math worksheet and trying to explain, you know, "Okay class, we're only going to do the even numbers today, and make sure you show your work," and before she even finished the sentence, I had already scribbled down answers for the first five questions. And they were usually wrong because I didn't actually listen to what we were supposed to do, I just wanted to get it done and move on to the next thing. 

So, yeah, my parents still talk about those elementary school conferences like they were a battleground. It was exhausting for them, I'm sure. But it definitely proves this was happening way, way before I hit 12 or started middle school. It's just how I've always been wired, way before I ever stepped foot in an x-ray lab.
